headline: France Gets Budget Warning as Fitch Turns Negative on Rating
author: William Horobin

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- France's credit score was put on a negative outlook by Fitch Ratings, in an unscheduled move that highlights the country's struggle to fix its public finances.

The change "reflects a deterioration since our August 2026 review comprising weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit," the company said in a statement late on Friday. "These worsen debt dynamics from an already weak starting point. Persistent political fragmentation and a challenging social backdrop increase the difficulty of delivering sustained fiscal consolidation."
France remains at A+ at Fitch, on par with Portugal and Belgium, and six notches above junk.
The announcement arrives on the eve of another weekend of protests in cities including Paris. Authorities are trying to contain violence after large-scale riots earlier this month.
"Fitch believes that developments in the country warrant such a deviation from the calendar," adding that its next scheduled review of France should conclude by the end of February.

The verdict is the latest indictment of France's inability to find a way to contain its swelling debt burden, which put the nation at the forefront of bond market anxiety over the past weeks. French yields have risen more than any other in the developed world this month, hitting the highest level in 24 years.
"We estimate the cumulative fiscal adjustment needed to stabilize debt has risen to around 3.5% of GDP, from 3.0% in August," Fitch said.

The country's ever-increasing debt mountain is fueled by a deficit set to blow out to 5.4% of economic output this year. Political gridlock, slumping growth and rising interest costs have derailed attempts at consolidation.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a finance bill to sharply constrain spending and raise tax revenues to meet a deficit goal of 5% next year, but the blueprint's future is uncertain as he has no majority in parliament.

Opposition groups are unwilling to compromise as they focus on presidential elections six months from now. Leading candidates from the far-left to the far-right are proposing radical changes in policy, including a lower retirement age and vast tax hikes for business.

The heightened uncertainty has caused a closely watched gauge of bond risk to rise to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis. The spread between 10-year yields in France and Germany, the region's safe asset, reached 178 basis points this month, compared to just 85 basis points at the start of September before the selloff picked up. It was around 165 on Friday.

Fitch's "assessment underlines the pressing need to pass a responsible budget before the end of the year that keeps our public finances on the path to recovery, by bringing the deficit down to 5%," French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said in a statement on Friday. "The government remains fully committed to fiscal consolidation. At a time of global uncertainty, it is vital that businesses and investors have a clear sense of direction."
